title: How to use this guide
summary: This booklet is for coaches. It's how you help Brand Ambassadors become competent, confident, and independent.
body:
This booklet gives every coach the sales impacts and campaign topics each Brand Ambassador needs to know to become competent, confident, and independent on their campaign.

It has 4 sections:
1. Coaching
2. Campaign Knowledge impacts
3. Sales systems
4. Industry impacts

How to use it:
- Know the content so you can find things fast. Study and practise each impact yourself before you run it.
- Always check the latest updates from your campaign.
- Run impacts for your students so they can take notes and learn.
- Aim to run every impact on the whiteboard in prime time.
- Never hand this booklet to anyone until they've reached stage 3.

Some students need the same impact 10 times. Some get it after 3. Keep running the topics until your students can apply them on their own.
key_takeaways: Study and practise each impact before you run it.
Check the latest campaign updates.
Run impacts on the whiteboard in prime time.
The booklet is for Stage 3 and above only.

title: Coaching Skills
summary: Coaching unlocks what's already in a person. Your role is to help them learn, not to tell them what to do.
body:
Coaching is helping someone make a change, learn something new, or hit their goals. Your role as a coach is to help them improve their own game — help them learn, don't just tell them what to do.

A great coach:
- Looks at how the person is performing
- Sets goals and targets with them
- Gives feedback all the time, not once
- Tracks their progress
- Shares tools and knowledge

The key skills:
- Listening
- Asking questions
- Building rapport
- Putting yourself in their shoes
- Summing up and reflecting back
- Breaking limiting beliefs
- Staying focused
- Holding back the urge to just tell them
- Staying open-minded, never judging
- Giving feedback they can act on

Something to sit with: in business and in life, your relationships decide your progress, your success, and your happiness. As a coach, it's on you to open up better communication.
key_takeaways: Coaching unlocks potential and helps people learn.
Help them learn — don't just tell them.
Listening, questioning, and empathy come first.
Strong relationships drive results.

title: Competency Cycle
summary: Every skill goes through four learning stages: Unconscious Incompetence, Conscious Incompetence, Conscious Competence, Unconscious Competence. Your role as a coach is to spot which stage your student is in.
body:
Every skill you learn goes through four stages.

1) Unconscious Incompetence — you don't know that you don't know. Think of a kid who has never seen a bike.

2) Conscious Incompetence — you know you can't do it yet. The kid sees others ride and wants to learn.

3) Conscious Competence — you can do it, but you still have to think about it. The kid can ride, but falls off the moment they stop paying attention.

4) Unconscious Competence — the skill is automatic. You don't think about it anymore. In fact, thinking too hard about it can break it.

Your role as a coach: figure out which stage your student is in, and match your words to it.

- Unconscious Incompetent: teach and give feedback until they understand the skill.
- Conscious Incompetent: give detailed feedback until they can do it.
- Conscious Competent: check in now and then until it becomes automatic.
- Unconscious Competent: step in with feedback when they get lazy or complacent.
key_takeaways: Stage 1: you don't know what you don't know.
Stage 2: you know the gap is there.
Stage 3: you can do it, but you have to think.
Stage 4: the skill runs on its own.

title: First-Time Coaching Tips
summary: Coaching for the first time? Know your students, plan your sessions, keep it simple and fun, and never stop learning yourself.
body:
Get to know your students. Chat with them 100%. Learn what they expect, find their goals, and shape your coaching around each person.

Never stop learning. Study sales, the cause, the industry, and yourself. Read books. Listen to podcasts. You can't pour from an empty cup.

Keep it simple. One clear message. Content that matters to them. Short but complete, and easy to take notes on.

Make it fun. Teach and motivate people at the same time. Balance hard work with fun. Find your own style.

Plan your sessions. Be organised, set a goal for each session, and recap at the end.

Watch other coaches. Study their body language (B.L.) and tone of voice (T.O.V.). Ask them for tips.

Know the learning styles: Kinesthetic (doing), Auditory (hearing), Visual (seeing). People learn differently.

Have standards. Look sharp, come prepared, share your own story — the ups and the downs.
key_takeaways: Know your students and coach each one their way.
Plan every session. Keep it simple and fun.
Watch other coaches and keep learning yourself.
People learn in different styles — adjust to them.

title: 8 Steps to Success
summary: The 8 basics of a winning career: attitude, reliability, prep, effort, territory, mindset, goals, and control.
body:
1. POSITIVE ATTITUDE — Success is 99% attitude, 1% ability. Make the way you think work for you.

2. BE RELIABLE — Manage your time. Showing up on time shows discipline. Keep your word.

3. BE PREPARED — Listen, Learn, Apply. Plan your day before it starts.

4. 100% EFFORT — This is your business. Give an extra 10% all the time and the results will surprise you.

5. WORK YOUR TERRITORY CORRECTLY — Don't pre-judge an area. The tough ones can be gold mines.

6. SAFEGUARD YOUR ATTITUDE — The average person has 65,000 thoughts a day, and 90% are negative. Take control of your thoughts.

7. KNOW YOUR GOALS & WHY — Set short-term and long-term goals. Keep your reason in front of you.

8. TAKE CONTROL — Be confident. Own your future. The way you dress, walk, and talk should show ambition.
key_takeaways: 99% attitude, 1% ability.
Show up on time, prepared, giving 100%.
Work the whole territory — don't pre-judge.
Set your goals and take control.

title: Prime Time
summary: Prime Time is set time in the office and the field where the results happen. Treat it like the most important hours of your day.
body:
OFFICE PRIME TIME — your chance to sit in on impacts, role play, learn from top performers, and grow.
- Role play scenarios
- Practise your pitch
- Run impacts
- Take notes
- Triangle coaching
- Sector setups
- Build relationships with top performers

FIELD PRIME TIME — the hours when most people are home from work or school. Usually late afternoon and evening. These are your peak hours.
- Follow the systems
- Believe in the Law of Averages
- Focus on your supporters
- Be the best version of yourself
- Watch others work, and let others watch you
- Use what you've learned

TYPES OF IMPACTS to run in Prime Time: Sales, Quality & Supporter Care, Campaign Knowledge, Leadership, Mentality, Industry.

How do you know which one to run? Break everyone's day down at the end of the day and see what needs work.
key_takeaways: Prime Time is your peak performance window.
In the office: learn, role play, connect.
In the field: follow the systems and bring your best.
Break days down to pick tomorrow's impacts.

title: Running Impacts
summary: An impact is a short, simple teaching session that makes a real difference to a BA's skillset. You can run one anywhere, anytime.
body:
WHAT — An impact is a topic that makes a BA better at what they do. Short, clear, to the point, and easy to remember.

WHEN — Anytime, anywhere. Impacts are a big part of Prime Time. Run them at social meetings, on the way to the field, or in the meeting room.

HOW — In the office, grab a whiteboard and marker. Anywhere else, use pen and paper or the COD stages. Take as long or as short as you need. Get the group talking, not just listening.

WATCH FOR:
- Don't let new people hide at the back.
- Keep eye contact. Don't talk to the board with your back turned.
- Speak TO the group, not AT them.
- Write clearly.
- Be confident. Enjoy it.
- Make it interactive.

REPETITION — "Repetition is the mother of skill." Some people need 10 repetitions. Some need 3. Both are fine.

PARTICIPATION — Pull in as many people as you can. Ask questions that make them think. Teach them how to take good notes.

ASSESS — Have them show the skill, recap what they learned, answer questions, and role play it.
key_takeaways: Impacts are short, clear, and to the point.
Run them anywhere — and get the group involved.
Repetition plus participation builds the skill.
Always check they actually got it.

title: How to Prepare a Great Impact
summary: A great impact takes prep: a plan, the right materials, practice, and a recap. That's how you create an impact instead of just talking.
body:
THE STANDARD — Everyone takes notes. You deliver clear content and a message that's easy to remember. That's what CREATING AN IMPACT means.

WHAT YOU NEED:
- A plan
- Notes to back yourself up
- Board marker (plus a spare)
- Extra pens for the audience
- Your image
- A whiteboard if needed
- Real knowledge on the topic
- Confidence
- The systems
- Results — they give you credibility

EVERY IMPACT SHOULD HAVE:
- Detailed content
- One clear, simple message
- A practical part — practise what was just taught
- A recap to check they understood

HOW TO BUILD UP TO DELIVERING ONE:
1st time: take notes. 2nd: add extra notes and refresh. 3rd: watch how it's delivered — body language (BL) and tone of voice (TOV). 4th: practise with a colleague. 5th: run it for real people, with your coach watching.

CREATIVE FORMATS: a game, impact cards, group activity, role play, competition, open forum, quiz, Q&A, case study, brainstorming. Mix it up.
key_takeaways: Come prepared: plan, materials, knowledge, confidence.
Every impact = content + message + practice + recap.
Build up in steps: watch, practise, then run it with your coach watching.
Switch formats to keep people engaged.

title: Types of Impacts
summary: There are six categories of impacts: Sales, Quality & Supporter Care, Campaign Knowledge, Leadership, Mentality, and Industry. Use them like a menu to plan your sessions.
body:
There are six kinds of impacts. Together they cover everything a BA needs.

SALES IMPACTS: S.E.E. principle, the 5 steps, Relating, L.O.A., G.I.F.T.S., Features & Benefits, Types of supporters, Hook lines, Hot Spots, the Objection Cycle, Timing the Close, Working different territories, Breaking days down, Understanding KPIs.

QUALITY & SUPPORTER CARE: the Sign-up process, Rehash, What Good Looks Like, No Shows, Why quality matters, Do's & Don'ts, Understanding churn, Long-term supporters, Avoiding fails and missed sign-ups, Behaviours of top BAs.

CAMPAIGN KNOWLEDGE: the National Deaf Children's Society, the problem and the solution, the PAFB and the Solicitation Statement, 5 Star Supporters, Who Not to Sign Up, the Welcome Call, and how the sign-up and the direct debit work.

LEADERSHIP: What is leadership, Standards, G.R.A.S.P, Running sectors, How to coach, Territory management, Recruitment, Goal setting, Finances, Personal development, Planning, Developing people, Team development, Core vs Average.

MENTALITY: the 8 steps, Winning mentality, Fixed vs Growth mindset, 3 types of days, Habits, Mastering skills, What you control vs what you don't, Emotional vs logical, Solution finding, S.W.O.T., Emotional intelligence.

INDUSTRY: Face-to-face fundraising, Direct vs Indirect, Marketing, Regular giving, the Charity sector.
key_takeaways: The 6 impact categories cover the whole BA skillset.
Mix categories across the week — don't run one type only.
Use this list as a menu to plan tomorrow's session.

title: 7 Presentation Skills
summary: How to hold a room when you present: body language, posture, positioning, voice, fillers, and space.
body:
BODY LANGUAGE (Face/Hands): Make eye contact across the whole room, not just one side. Match your face to your words. No fidgeting with markers, no hands in pockets.

BODY LANGUAGE (Posture): Stand up straight. It helps your voice carry and makes you look confident. Change your posture when you move to a new point.

BODY LANGUAGE (Positioning): Plant your feet. Don't pace back and forth. Only sit down with very small groups. Never turn your back on the room.

VOICE (Volume/Pitch/Pauses): Project your voice. Change your pitch to stress the big points. Pauses give people time to think — don't be scared of silence.

VOICE (Fillers): Watch your fillers — 'um, ah, like, ok'. Don't rush the end of your sentences. Stay warm but professional. Make it sound like the first time you're saying it.

SPACE: Move among the group. Don't ignore any section of the room. Stand close to the class unless you're using the board.

EXTRA TIPS: Keep it short. Skip the jargon. Practise. Watch great presenters (TED talks). Show enthusiasm — smiling is infectious!
key_takeaways: Body language and tone of voice = 93% of communication.
Project your voice, vary your pitch, use pauses.
Move through the room — don't pace.
Show enthusiasm — smile!

title: Role Playing
summary: Practise real door scenarios out loud. It builds confidence, makes you fluent, and teaches you to find answers fast.
body:
WHY ROLE PLAY:
- It pushes your brain to find answers
- It builds confidence and fluency
- It sharpens your selling skills
- It helps you stand on your own
- It makes you a problem-solver

WHEN — Morning sales coaching, on the way to the field, and between doors if you need it.

WHO — Owners, Assistant Owners, coaches, BAs. Everyone.

HOW TO ROLE PLAY WELL:
- Work on ONE thing at a time until it's fluent.
- Use 10/10/10: 10x intro, 10x presentation, 10x short story, and so on.
- Listen more than you talk.
- Repeat until body language and tone of voice get better.
- Celebrate every small win (high-five, fist bump).
- Give honest, helpful feedback.
- Ask if they're ready to move on.
- Once one piece is fluent, mix in different scenarios.

Set expectations and a learning goal before you start. Follow up in the field. Recap at the end of the day.
key_takeaways: Use the 10/10/10 rule to get fluent.
One thing at a time.
Repeat it, then celebrate the small wins.
Role play on the way to the field.

title: Pitch Doctor
summary: Help your students find the weak spots in their pitch. Focus on body language, tone of voice, and delivery — not just the words.
body:
Some people think once you learn your pitch, you're done practising. Wrong. Mastering sales takes constant coaching, just like any sport. Your role as a coach is to find the weak spots and help make them strong.

KEY POINTS TO LOOK FOR:
- Are we impulsing in the introduction?
- Are we taking control?
- Are we assuming the sign-up?
- Are we sizzling the cause?
- Are our impulses exciting enough?

Focus on Body Language and Tone of Voice. They carry 93% of communication. Words are only 7%.

DELIVERY:
- TONE OF VOICE — check it often. Don't rush the pace.
- STANCE — stand steady. Don't pace around.
- FUN — more fun means more learning.
- ATMOSPHERE — build people's confidence. Have other coaches chime in.
- TIME — spend as long as it takes.

Remember the loop: Practice builds Confidence. Confidence builds Results. Results build more confidence.
key_takeaways: Body Language and Tone of Voice carry 93% of communication.
Check the impulses, the control, and the sizzle.
Keep it fun and build their confidence.
Repeat it until they use it for real.

title: Setting the Day Up
summary: Top results with fewer problems come from how you set up: before the office, in the office, and on the way to the field.
body:
BEFORE THE OFFICE — Wake up earlier. Get your image right first. Make lunch the night before. Leave early so you walk in ready.

IN THE OFFICE — Welcome everyone. Get to know the people around you. Bring a notebook and take good notes. Be proactive. Plan your day. Use Prime Time to coach others and to learn. Set your sector up before you head out.

ON THE WAY TO THE FIELD — Talk through the sector goals. Talk through each person's goals. Share tips on territories, supporters, and door scenarios. Leave room for downtime too: get to know people. Share success stories. Energise people with teaching, stories, competition, and mini challenges.
key_takeaways: Wake up earlier, arrive earlier.
Plan in the office and use Prime Time.
Talk sector and personal goals on the way out.
Mix work with downtime to build the team.

title: S.E.E. Principle
summary: Smile, Eye contact, Enthusiasm. It's the base of every doorstep conversation you'll ever have.
body:
SMILE — a smile is contagious. It's welcoming, friendly, and polite. It starts the relationship the second the door opens.

EYE CONTACT — it builds trust. It shows you're confident and honest.

ENTHUSIASM — it makes people curious. It makes you different from the last person who knocked. It pulls people in.

Your tone of voice is key. Aim to make a 1 minute friend at every door.
key_takeaways: Smile = relationship.
Eye contact = trust.
Enthusiasm = what makes you different.
Make a 1-minute friend at every door.

title: The 5 Steps
summary: Every sign-up follows the same path: Introduction, Present the Problem, The Solution, The Close, Rehash.
body:
1. INTRODUCTION — First impressions. Ask engaging questions. Who we are and why we're here: "Hi there, how are you doing? I'm here on behalf of the National Deaf Children's Society. We're on a mission to get sign language into all the schools, do you know any sign language?"

2. PRESENT THE PROBLEM — Use need. Paint the picture and invite compassion. Pause and gain agreement. Take your time, do not rush: "Every day in the UK, three babies are born deaf — and most deaf children are born to hearing parents. So you can imagine how tough that is, right?"

3. THE SOLUTION — What we do. Reset the energy first, then sell the solution. K.I.S.S — Keep it Short & Simple. Speak with pride, passion and feeling, and thank them after they agree: "What we do as a charity is amazing — we go into schools and homes to help parents and teachers communicate with deaf children, so they can do simple things like read a bedtime story."

4. THE CLOSE — The ask. They already know why you are here. Point at the presenter card and show the amount. Small amount, huge difference. Be clear, be confident, be concise: "Knowing the difference you can make, can we get your help as well? My job is super simple — I send a form to your phone, you choose what you want to contribute, and you get a welcome call in the next 30–60 minutes."

5. REHASH — Make it stick. Reassure long-term commitment, cement the support so it lasts beyond today, and make them feel like the hero: "Before I go, let me make sure you know exactly what happens next — so there are no surprises." Then the Pop Quiz (monthly amount, frequency, start date: 1st / 8th / 15th / 22nd, why NDCS makes a Welcome Call) and the 3 Thank You's — from you: "Thank you for taking the time to stop and support children and families supported by NDCS today." From NDCS: "On behalf of NDCS, thank you for choosing to make a difference every single month." From the children and families: "Every month when your donation goes out, your bank will often send you a notification. That notification means a child somewhere is getting support because of you."

Gain agreement before you ask. No agreement, no close.
key_takeaways: The 5 steps: Introduction, the Problem, the Solution, the Close, Rehash.
Gain agreement before you ask — no agreement, no close.
The rehash is what makes supporters stay long-term.

title: Ice Breakers
summary: Start the conversation with a funny story, an open question, or a compliment — based on what you notice at the door.
body:
An ice breaker warms up the conversation. Use what you SEE, HEAR, and SMELL to figure out who you're talking to.

Examples — say something about the garden, the football shirt, the dog, the smell of cooking, the weather, the sign by the door.

Stay away from touchy topics: politics, sex, religion.

Or use the question in our opener: "do you know any sign language?" — then listen, and relate to what they tell you.

Keep it light, real, and quick.
key_takeaways: Use what you SEE, HEAR, and SMELL.
Funny story, open question, or compliment.
Never politics, sex, or religion.

title: Relating & Hot Spots
summary: Listen for what the supporter cares about — their hot spots — then shape your pitch around it.
body:
SPOT THE HOT SPOTS — Listen, enjoy the chat, ask questions, then shape what you say around it with enthusiasm.

Work out what kind of supporter is in front of you before you pitch.

Talk about what they love and what gets them excited. People love talking about themselves — let them.

Be real, honest, and friendly the whole time.
key_takeaways: Listen for what they love.
Point your Impulses at their hot spots.
Stay real and friendly.

title: G.I.F.T.S. Impulse Factors
summary: Five impulses that raise interest levels when BAs aren't getting to the close: Generosity, Indifference, Feel Good Factor, Tone of Voice / Body Language, Support.
body:
G — GENEROSITY: The tremendous difference their support WILL make. Give them a BIG 'Thank You' when they agree to become an ongoing donor. Make sure the donor feels good about themselves for their selflessness.

I — INDIFFERENCE: People love to buy but hate to be sold to; be genuine and natural, NOT pushy. Don't give the impression that you are desperate. Step back when you get supporter concerns, keep out of the donor's personal space, and learn to look relaxed.

F — FEEL GOOD FACTOR: Paint mental pictures of what the charity is trying to overcome. Evoke empathy in the donor about why their support is so very important. Use emotive language and tone of voice.

T — TONE OF VOICE / BODY LANGUAGE: Stress keywords and phrases. Use their name, if offered to you. Use assumption language. Match your body language with what you are saying — nod when asking 'yes' questions.

S — SUPPORT: People love to support when others are supporting too. They do not like to be the first or only one supporting. "We've had great support from people in this area."
key_takeaways: Generosity, Indifference, Feel Good Factor, Tone of Voice / Body Language, Support.
Be genuine and natural — NOT pushy.
People love to support when others are supporting too.

title: Features vs Benefits
summary: A feature is what the campaign offers. A benefit is what the supporter gets out of it. You sell the benefit, every time.
body:
A FEATURE is something the campaign has or does. A BENEFIT is what the supporter actually gets out of it. Features tell. Benefits sell.

So every time you name a feature, turn it into the win for the person in front of you.

EXAMPLE (Feature to Benefit), straight from our solution line: "we go into schools and homes to help parents and teachers communicate with deaf children" is the feature — "so they can do simple things like read a bedtime story" is the benefit.

And show real passion and excitement when you say it. Enthusiasm rubs off on people.
key_takeaways: Features tell. Benefits sell.
Turn every feature into what the supporter gets.
Know the campaign: the problem, the solution, the £12 a month ask and how the sign-up works.

title: Hook Lines
summary: Hook lines are smart questions that get small yeses through the pitch, so the supporter talks themselves into it.
body:
A hook line is a smart question that gets a small agreement. Stack enough small yeses and the big yes gets easy.

Use hook lines in all 5 steps of your pitch to build commitment as you go.

Use one right before you close, to lock in agreement.

POWER OF THE PEN: use a pen to point at the presenter card. Their eyes follow the pen. That's you choosing what they focus on.

Hook lines from our pitch:
- "Do you know any sign language?" (the introduction)
- "So you can imagine how tough that is, right?" (after the problem — pause and gain agreement)
- Nod when you ask a 'yes' question — match your body language to what you're saying.
key_takeaways: Hook lines = small yeses all through the pitch.
Use them in every step.
Point with the pen to steer their focus.

title: Objection Cycle
summary: A concern usually means they're listening. Listen first, find the real concern, respond with clarity: Feel, Relate, Felt, Found, Re-close.
body:
A supporter concern is often a sign of interest. If they're raising it, they're listening. Listen first. Find the real concern. Respond with clarity.

THE CYCLE:
1. FEEL — Let the donor know you care about the concern. Empathise with them.
2. RELATE — Build a slight bond so it sounds natural. Make them feel great here.
3. FELT — Let the donor know this concern has previously been raised by other people.
4. FOUND — Show the difference their small contribution will make to families.
5. RE-CLOSE — Having listened, empathised and reassured — close them.
key_takeaways: A concern means interest, not rejection.
Feel, Relate, Felt, Found, Re-close.
Listen and reassure first — then re-close.

title: Types of Objections
summary: Some concerns you can address and some you can't. Learn both lists, and learn to spot interest signals and leaving signals while you talk.
body:
CAN ADDRESS: other charities; one-off; bank details or don't want to give my details; I'll do it online; more information.

CANNOT ADDRESS: no door to door; no direct debit; cannot afford; not interested. Thank them and move on.

Whatever comes at you: stay calm. Smile. Be yourself. See it from their side. Offer solutions. Ask questions. Never panic and never look desperate.

INTEREST SIGNALS: they use your name, nod along, finish your sentences, lean in, or ask "how does that work?"

LEAVING SIGNALS: no smile, no eye contact, straight face, arms crossed, looking away.

If you see leaving signals, change tactic. Change your pace, ask a personal question, or hand them something to look at.
key_takeaways: Can address: other charities, one-off, bank details, online, more information.
Cannot address: no door to door, no direct debit, cannot afford, not interested.
Watch for interest signals vs leaving signals.

title: Handling Objections
summary: Three steps for any objection: agree and empathise, investigate, then solve.
body:
1. AGREE & EMPATHISE. Make the supporter feel heard first.

2. INVESTIGATE. Ask questions to find the real reason behind the objection. What's their biggest worry?

3. SOLVE. Give real answers: how the direct debit works — £12 a month, a quick form to their phone, starting in the next 3–4 weeks — and reassure them.

DON'T:
- Argue
- Get defensive
- Talk over them

DO:
- Slow down
- Take notes
- Check they're happy before you move on
key_takeaways: Agree, then investigate, then solve.
Ask questions before you offer answers.
Reassurance closes more than features do.

title: Common Objections — Real Life
summary: The concerns you'll hear most at the door, and the redirect scripts that work. Know these cold before you knock.
body:
A redirect is a buying sign — not a no. Turn it, then re-close it.

ONE-OFF DONATION? "Thank you, that's really generous! What we're actually asking is a small amount regularly so we can plan and budget — usually £12 a month for 12–18 months. Knowing that, could you squeeze us in as well?"

CAN I DO IT ONLINE? "Absolutely — it's all a quick online form! I jot down basic details, send the form to your phone, get a reference number, and your direct debit starts in the next 3–4 weeks."

SMALL AMOUNT? "I know it doesn't sound like a lot — but when a lot of people do a small amount, it makes a huge difference. Can we count on your support as well?"

OTHER CHARITIES, BANK DETAILS, MORE INFORMATION: concerns we can address — run Feel, Relate, Felt, Found, Re-close.

NO DOOR TO DOOR, NO DIRECT DEBIT, CANNOT AFFORD, NOT INTERESTED: we cannot address these. Thank them and move on.
key_takeaways: Know the redirect scripts cold: one-off, online, small amount.
A redirect is a buying sign — not a no.
Cannot afford or not interested: thank them and move on.

title: Closing Effectively
summary: Close with clarity: direct, slow, warm and long term — then tell them what happens next.
body:
The close is the moment the supporter decides to get involved. They already know you're going to ask — so ask clearly.

How to close well:
- Be direct and clear. No mumbling. No trailing off.
- Slow down and speak up. Speed = doubt. The close is not the place to rush.
- Eye contact + gratitude. Hold their eyes. Stay warm. Keep indifference — no big deal.
- Ask confidently — long term: chipping in £12 a month for as long as they can. "Can we count on your support as well?"
- Tell them what happens next: a quick form to their phone, a few details, and the direct debit starts in the next 3–4 weeks.

The key move: ask for the sign-up with confidence, then go quiet. Let them answer.
key_takeaways: Be direct and clear — no mumbling, no trailing off.
Slow down, speak up, hold eye contact.
Ask confidently for the long term.
Tell them what happens next.

title: Mastering The Close
summary: Why BAs don't close — confidence, fear of rejection, poor example, not enough agreement — and the rule that fixes it.
body:
Diagnose it first. There are 4 reasons BAs don't close:

1. CONFIDENCE — You don't back yourself. So you mumble, trail off, half-ask.
2. FEAR OF REJECTION — You have personalised the no. So you avoid the ask to avoid the sting.
3. POOR EXAMPLE — You've never seen it done right. Bad coaching gets copied.
4. NOT ENOUGH AGREEMENT — You didn't build it. No yeses on the way up = no yes at the top.

THE RULE: An unclear close isn't a soft no. It's a sign-up you left at the door — and a deaf child who didn't get supported.
key_takeaways: Four reasons BAs don't close: confidence, fear of rejection, poor example, not enough agreement.
No yeses on the way up = no yes at the top.
An unclear close isn't a soft no — it's a sign-up left at the door.

title: Timing The Close
summary: The Impulse Curve: close above the giving line. Impulse rises, peaks, then dies — close at the peak. Slightly early beats too late.
body:
THE IMPULSE CURVE — Close above the giving line. Impulse rises, peaks, then dies — close at the peak. Slightly early beats too late.

So read the signals. Has the supporter agreed with the key points? Are they leaning in? Are they finishing your sentences?

Use assertive language: "You probably noticed this, but…" It gets them agreeing with you.

Get them agreeing with everything you have said before you ask for the close.
key_takeaways: Close at the peak of the impulse curve.
Slightly early beats too late.
Watch for the signals.
Get agreement on everything, then ask.

title: Law of Averages (L.O.A.)
summary: The more people you speak to, the more sign-ups you get. Work ethic beats talent.
body:
"The law of averages is not an excuse to be average. It is a reminder to control the inputs."

The Law of Averages is simple: do something enough times and a ratio shows up. Talk to 10 people, get 1 yes. Talk to 10 more, get another yes. And so on.

That is why work ethic always beats talent.

In sales this ratio is called your Conversion Rate. It gets better as your skills, work ethic, and attitude get better.

Look for positive people and work positive leads. Never take a 'No' personally — it is just part of the ratio.

Know your numbers. Track them and adjust. And always ask who you can circle back to.
key_takeaways: Speak to more people, get more sign-ups.
Track your numbers and let them guide you.
Don't take 'No' personally.
Work ethic beats talent.

title: Believing in L.O.A.
summary: Believe in the Law of Averages and you stay calm and logical. Your attitude drives your sign-ups — never the other way around.
body:
When you believe in the Law of Averages, you can get the result you want without getting frustrated. A slow morning is just numbers waiting to catch up.

It teaches you to think in a logical, numbers-driven way.

The more people you speak to each day, the more sign-ups you get. Simple.

Let your ATTITUDE decide your sign-ups. Never let your sign-ups decide your attitude.

Move with urgency. Every minute you save is another person you can speak to.
key_takeaways: Attitude drives sign-ups — not the reverse.
Stay logical, don't get emotional.
Urgency means more conversations.
Trust the system.

title: Types of Territories
summary: There are three broad territory types: low income, mid income and high income. Each one responds differently, so you work each one differently.
body:
THE TYPES — Low income, Mid income, High income.

Why learn your territory:
- You can perform anywhere
- You know which Impulses to use, so you go in confident
- You understand how supporters in that area act
- You build emotional intelligence

Different Impulses work in different territories. Test them in every sector you work.

And don't pre-judge. Some of the toughest-looking territories turn out to be gold mines.
key_takeaways: 3 broad territory types.
Each one needs a different mix of Impulses.
Test Impulses sector by sector.
Don't pre-judge.

title: Types of Supporters
summary: There are 4 types of supporters: Direct, Sensitive, Ingenious, Conscious. Spot which one you have, then mirror match them.
body:
Not every supporter is the same. There are 4 types, and each one needs a different you.

DIRECT — they get straight to the point. Match their pace. Cut to the chase.

SENSITIVE — often the older generation, a bit hesitant. Slow down. Reassure them. Build trust first.

INGENIOUS — bubbly people who laugh easily. They will sign up if they like you. Have fun with them.

CONSCIOUS — they want facts. Be precise. Have your stats and campaign details ready.

MIRROR MATCH — copy the supporter's voice, tone, and pace. When you sound like them, they feel understood.
key_takeaways: There are 4 supporter types.
Mirror match their voice and pace.
Change what you say to fit their style.
The right approach means more sign-ups.

title: Building New Habits
summary: About 40% of what you do every day is habit. Build the right ones — start tiny, and only one or two at a time.
body:
Habits run about 40% of your behaviour. That means almost half your day is on autopilot. Build the right habits and the autopilot works for you.

The rules:
- Start incredibly small — just 1% better a day.
- Grow it in small steps.
- Break big habits into chunks.
- Slipped up? Get back on track fast. One miss is fine. Two is a new habit.
- Pick a pace you can keep up.
- The 21-day rule: it takes about 21 days for a habit to stick. So work on one or two max — not five.
key_takeaways: Start small — 1% a day.
One or two habits at a time, no more.
Give it 21 days to stick.
If you slip, get back on track fast.

title: Consistency
summary: Consistency is a behaviour, not a mood. Make a plan, stick to it, and let sales become second nature.
body:
Consistency is about what you do, not how you feel. Have a plan and follow it — even on the days you don't feel like it.

The keys:
- Make a plan and stick to it.
- Prioritise — do what matters first.
- Manage your emotions. Don't let one bad door decide your day.
- Know your numbers.
- Cut out distractions.
- Train four muscles: self-awareness, self-regulation, self-discipline, self-motivation.

Be patient with the process. And set high standards — for yourself and for the team.
key_takeaways: Plan it, prioritise it, keep your head.
Know your numbers.
Cut out distractions.
High standards for you and the team.

title: Supporter Care — Do's & Don'ts
summary: The supporter's experience of the brand starts with you. Protect it at all times.
body:
DON'TS:
- Be pushy
- Mislead or lie
- Be rude, aggressive, or unprofessional
- Swear or use inappropriate icebreakers
- Wear your badge outside field hours
- Drop confidential supporter names
- Represent the brand under the influence
- Interact inappropriately with children
- Handle a supporter's card during the sign-up
- Smoke, eat, or drink alcohol in branded clothing
- Enter homes uninvited
- Promote competitors
- Sign up anyone on the Who Not to Sign Up list: under 30, over 75, anyone vulnerable or not able to make their own decisions, existing supporters, anyone under the influence of alcohol, friends & family
- Post on social media as a campaign BA without permission

DO'S:
- Be polite, courteous, and professional
- Wear branded clothing the right way, per the guidelines
- Keep your ID badge visible at all times
- Leave every door on a positive note
- Make it clear who you represent — the donor must always hear the Solicitation Statement
- Take extra time with vulnerable people
- Always thank people, even when they don't sign up
key_takeaways: Brand image comes first, always.
Polite, professional, in branded clothing.
No pushy tactics, no shortcuts.
Leave a positive last impression.

title: Mis-selling & Fraud
summary: Mis-selling gets you removed. No tricking people, no fake details, no false promises to close.
body:
Here is what counts as MIS-SELLING:
- Misleading vulnerable people (elderly people, minors, people who don't speak English well, hearing impaired)
- Getting the facts, the amount, or how the direct debit works wrong on purpose or by being sloppy
- Pretending to be a supporter
- Changing a supporter's details without their permission
- Signing up an existing supporter under different details
- Signing up the same person more than once
- Telling a supporter they can cancel straight away just to get the sign-up
- Presenting a regular direct debit as a one-off donation
- Leaving out the Solicitation Statement — the donor must always be made aware that the PAFB pays for professional fundraisers

Fake sign-ups hurt the charity and cost the marketing company real money.

No pushy or aggressive selling. If someone says no, you don't keep pushing. Bad cases mean removal from the campaign.
key_takeaways: Mis-selling = removal.
Take extra care with vulnerable people.
Never use false promises to close.
One sign-up per person — never duplicated.

title: Best Practices
summary: Sell the full value, talk long-term, and ask the right questions — that's how a sign-up sticks.
body:
These habits keep your supporters on board:

- Always rehash after the yes — what happens next, the Pop Quiz and the 3 Thank You's. If they still have questions after you leave, they'll cancel.
- Ask for £12 a month, long term, and sign up at the amount they chose. Never push an amount so far that it won't last.
- Sell yourself on the cause first. If you believe it, they will.
- Remind them of the difference their gift makes. It's not just a donation — it's being part of the cause.
- Ask questions to check they really understand.
- Talk long-term: what their support adds up to over a year, not just a month.
- Show them how the direct debit works: it starts in the next 3–4 weeks, on the 1st, 8th, 15th or 22nd.
- Talk about one part of the cause's work that matters to them.
- Ask them to stay with it long enough to see the difference.
- Never say 'try it for a month' — that plants short-term thinking.
- Ask the RIGHT questions: what matters to them, and why the cause connects.
- Mention how they can tell friends and family about the cause.
key_takeaways: A proper rehash stops cancellations.
Sign up at the amount they chose and talk long-term.
Ask the right questions about what matters to them.
Mention how they can tell friends and family about the cause.

title: Call Back Tracker
summary: Your call back tracker is how you work a territory right — log everything, aim for 10 call backs a day.
body:
What it's for:
- Working the territory and saving time
- Logging appointments and who to go back to
- Counting how many people you spoke to
- Knowing your numbers
- Breaking the day down

What to write down:
- Sector basics: your name, postcode, date, sector leader, time
- Street names in CAPITALS, plus house numbers
- Callback notes: their name, the dog's name, what you talked about, what time to return
- People spoken to, pitched, closed
- When you arrive, leave, and take breaks

Callback tips:
- Only talk to the decision maker.
- Stay casual when setting one up: 'I'll be at your neighbours till 7:30, will catch you later if I can.'
- Never PROMISE to come back — staying loose creates fear of loss.
- Aim for 10 callbacks a day.
- Do callbacks after 7pm, when people are home.

Fill it in neatly and carry a spare. Re-walk your territory the next day — that's how you get density.
key_takeaways: Write everything down for tomorrow.
Aim for 10 callbacks a day.
Callbacks after 7pm, decision maker only.
Re-walk the territory for density.

title: Breaking the Day Down
summary: Set a goal every hour instead of staring at the whole day. It keeps you focused and thinking with logic, not emotion.
body:
Why break the day into hours?
- It's easier to focus for 1 hour than for a whole day.
- You make logical decisions instead of emotional reactions.
- You stay focused longer.
- You learn to look forward, not back.

How to do it:
- Use the front or back of your call back tracker.
- Check it every hour in the field, and every night in the office.
- Set a goal every hour.
- Missed the hour's goal? Reset. Don't drag it into the next hour.
- Every hour is a new hour.

Track four things: Hours | People Spoken To | Short Stories | Closes.
key_takeaways: Set a goal every hour, fresh each hour.
Track spoken, stories, and closes hourly.
Focus on the process, not the result.
Logic beats emotion.

title: Weekly KPI Tracker
summary: Track your numbers every day for a week. The patterns tell you what to coach tomorrow and how to stop a dip before it starts.
body:
USE IT TO:
- Pick what to work on each day
- Spot repeating patterns and weak spots
- Find your strengths
- Check your own game and ask for extra coaching
- Plan impacts and topics
- Act early and dodge dips
- Build a solution-first habit
- Live the value: 'Enthusiasm powered by data'

WRITE DOWN EVERY DAY (copy your numbers from Field IQ): Doors (target 120–140), Spoken (80–90), Presented (20–25), Closed (15–20), Flow (5–7), Sign-ups (3–5). Add the time you started, your daily goal and your learning focus.

TOTAL = add up all your days. ANALYSIS = total divided by days = your ratio.

Then write your WEEKLY GOAL, what you ACHIEVED, and your WINS and IMPROVEMENTS.
key_takeaways: Your daily numbers build the weekly story.
Patterns show your strengths and weak spots.
Plan impacts from the data, not gut feel.
Enthusiasm powered by data.

title: 3 Types of Days
summary: Every day is Early, Steady, or Late. Each one tests you differently — late days build the bullet-proof mentality.
body:
EARLY DAYS — most of your sign-ups land before prime time. You're buzzing all day. It doesn't test your stamina. Anyone can perform on an early day.

STEADY DAYS — sign-ups come in at an even pace. The day feels normal. It doesn't test much either.

LATE DAYS — the sign-ups show up in the last hours. These test your attitude and your stamina. They're the best teachers:
- You learn the most about yourself
- They build a bullet-proof mentality
- They prove the L.O.A. and the systems work

Here's the gap between top BAs and average BAs: how they react to the type of day. Top performers stay logical and don't quit when the sign-ups come late.
key_takeaways: 3 day types: Early, Steady, Late.
Late days test you the most.
Bullet-proof mentality means you never quit.
Trust the system no matter the day.

title: Running Winning Sectors
summary: A winning sector starts before the first door. Prep everything, give a strong sector impact, and be on the bell all day.
body:
PREP BEFORE THE DAY:
- Maps ready — street viewed, highlighted, route planned.
- Sector impact written down, with positive examples ready to share.
- Teams planned out.
- Merch sorted — CB trackers, rec sheets, pitch cards.
- Badges ready for new BAs.

THE SECTOR IMPACT — what to hit:
- Show real passion about the territory.
- Share success stories from that area.
- The positives of the area.
- The USPs that work there.
- The Impulses that work there.
- How the day is going to play out.
- Goals, and who's accountable for what.

TIPS:
- Big SOU. Remember new BAs need more time than you do.
- Put the right people together.
- Guide the 'feeling' of the group.
- Refocus everyone as you get near the territory.
- Quick huddle when the sector starts.
- SOU straight to the first door.

WHAT MAKES THE DIFFERENCE:
- Be on the bell — with the sector or with your new person.
- Set small goals based on the process, not just the result.
- Keep tips, competitions, and rewards going all day.
- Bring vision, success, and fun.

BE THE EXAMPLE OF PASSION AND ENTHUSIASM EVERY DAY.
key_takeaways: Prep maps, merch, teams, and badges before the day.
Sector impact = stories, Impulses, USPs, goals.
Be on the bell.
Be the example every day.

title: Sector Feedback Form
summary: A simple checklist that helps you plan the sector, run it well, review it after, and build your next sector leaders.
body:
The Sector Feedback Form is a tool. Use it to:
- Get more planned and organised.
- Set every BA up with a focus for the day.
- Make sure people are learning and working at their best.
- Prep your impacts and tips for the day.
- Drive the sector to its best results.
- Give the day structure.
- Build confidence and independence in your people.
- Find answers to problems faster.
- Keep the balance between fun and business.
- Develop your next Sector Leaders.
- Break days down and mark off your maps.
- Review the day and deal with challenges.

WHAT TO TRACK FOR EACH BA:
- Name, stage, goal, what they achieved, territory plan, Impulses, tips.
- Their numbers: houses, spoken, pitched, closed, sign-ups.
- Plan for tomorrow: who, what, when. Plus impact, time, and who they're working with.

SECTOR REVIEW: Did the sector hit its goals? If yes — what worked? If no — what are you doing about it?

And share the positive stories: goals hit, PCs, people developing, LOA recognition, people advancing, top performers.
key_takeaways: Plan and review every sector with the form.
The structure builds your next sector leader.
Shout out the wins.
Break the day down every night.

title: Coaching New People — Day 1
summary: How to run a new BA's first day — morning, day, and evening — plus what to keep doing on days 2-6.
body:
Day 1 decides whether a new BA comes back. Here's how you run it.

MORNING:
- Give the office tour and show the systems.
- Explain our responsibility to the client and the brand.
- Explain why the ID badge matters.
- Walk through the MC schedule and roles.
- Explain why we celebrate wins (bells and gongs).
- Build their confidence. Day 1 is an experience, not a test. No pressure.
- Set a daily goal together.
- Get them ready for the hard parts before they happen.
- Follow the 8 steps from day 1.
- Introduce them to the team and to the top performers.
- Do not leave their side. This is the VELCRO EFFECT — you stick to them all day.

DURING THE DAY:
- Keep the conversation going.
- Get excited about every sign-up.
- Show them how you get past obstacles.
- Have them present to you around mid-day.
- Show them how to work a territory.

EVENING:
- Explain why we come back to the office.
- Congratulate them on a great first day.

DAYS 2-6: Keep coaching. Watch how they grow. Get them on a conference call with top BAs. Sit down every night to review the day and set goals together.
key_takeaways: Velcro effect: stay by their side all of day 1.
Run the day in three parts: morning, day, evening.
Set goals with them, not for them.
Connect them with top performers early.

title: Week 1 Coaching Plan
summary: A day-by-day plan for a new BA's first week — from the intro on day 1 to their first sign-ups on their own.
body:
Every day of week 1 has one clear focus. Follow the plan.

DAY 1 — BA Academy Day 1 (office): a full overview of the business, the direct sales industry and the career opportunities ahead. Earnings and incentives, Our Expectations, COD progression, and starting to study the sign-up process and presentation skills.

DAY 2 — BA Academy Day 2 (office): a deep dive into sales coaching so they're ready for their first day on badge. Knowledge about the charity, the 5 Steps word for word, Who Not to Sign Up, the PAFB and Solicitation Statement, the Welcome Call, the rehash, and the sales systems (S.E.E., G.I.F.T.S, BL, TOV).

DAY 3 — Practical Learning Day (field, shadowing their coach): Prime time → script 10/10/10, BL, sign up. On the way to the field → map, CB tracker, LOA, the 3 types of day. In the field → 40/20 principle, work ethic, breakdown.

DAY 4 — First day on badge: PT → GIFTS theory and examples, the objection cycle plus simple objections, role play. WTTF → qualifiers, games. Field → 40/20, time on doors, evening time, social.

DAY 5 — First days on badge: PT → closing, taking control, rehash. WTTF → the "better than yesterday" challenge. Field → 20/40, time on doors, the 8 steps.

DAY 6 — Badge Development & Consolidation: Saturday wake-up call and PT. Work Saturday the right way, finish strong, fill in the weekly tracker, plan next week.

DAY 7: Sunday planning. Contact the team, set goals and the agenda, communicate, and finish COD stage 1 → pass on Monday.

The first week is about building confidence, celebrating small wins, learning the basic systems, repeating them, and getting independent.
key_takeaways: Every day has one clear focus.
Days 1–2 are the BA Academy, Day 3 is the shadow day, Day 4 on is on badge.
Saturday is for finishing strong.
Sunday is for planning and talking to the team.

title: Month 1 Coaching Plan
summary: A week-by-week plan for a BA's first month — from passing COD 1 to growing as a leader.
body:
Month 1 takes a new BA from Stage 1 to Stage 3+ if you coach it week by week.

WEEK 1 — COD 1: Intro, product coaching, sales coaching, watching and being watched, 100% effort, student mentality, BAM attendance, pass COD 1, and start personal recruiting.

WEEK 2 — COD 2: Get comfortable with the sales process. Refine the pitch, work the field on their own, pass COD 2, understand the company structure, network, and plan the week.

WEEK 3 — COD 3: Show up strong every day. Get ready for advancement, set the example, pass COD 3, watch coaching being done, run sectors, master the sales systems.

WEEK 4 — COD 3+: Grow as a leader. Watch coaching methods, coach new BAs, run week 1 coaching, work with someone on stage 2, master sectors, run impacts, visit another office.

WEEK 5 — COD 3+: Watch impacts with a focus on BL and TOV. Build presentation skills, host new people, help others advance, work through the impact booklet, network, COD 3+, pick a team name and logo.

WEEK 6 — COD 4: Pass COD 3+. Keep learning, manage territory, grow yourself and your team, build confidence, take a road trip, appear in the company bulletin.

WEEK 7 — COD 4+: Office visit for the team. Find a mentor, get ready for your first road trip, COD 4 — team building and development.

WEEK 8 — COD 4+: Crew leadership. Network with Owners, mentor someone, qualify for trips, master coaching, build a name as the best coach around.
key_takeaways: Month 1 takes them from Stage 1 to 3+.
Every week has its own milestone.
By week 8 they should be pushing for Stage 4, Crew Leadership.
Never stop learning and reviewing.

title: Leadership — A Process, Not a Position
summary: A leader is someone who moves people to get great results. Keep a student mentality and you keep growing.
body:
Leaders get recognised for one thing: they move people to get great results. The skills that got you here matter, but leading takes more than being a great seller.

A student mentality is the key. Leaders lead by example and keep getting better. Your role is not to build a team of followers — it is to create more leaders.

A good leader also keeps a balance: you keep growing yourself while you grow your team.
key_takeaways: Leadership = influence plus results.
Never stop learning.
Build leaders, not followers.
Grow yourself and your team at the same time.

title: 5 Phases of Leadership Development
summary: The leader's growth path in 5 phases — from leading yourself to coaching leaders who build other leaders.
body:
You grow as a leader in 5 phases. Each one builds on the last.

1. LEAD YOURSELF FIRST — Get your own house in order: personal organisation, self-discipline, motivation, campaign knowledge, work ethic.

2. LEAD & COACH OTHERS — Create a vision, model the right behaviours, coach people to perform, learn to guide people.

3. COACH OTHERS INTO LEADERSHIP — Put development pathways in place, spot the gaps, coach advanced sales.

4. COACH LEADERS TO DEVELOP OTHERS — Run 'coach the coaches' sessions and advanced coaching.

5. COACH LEADERS TO DEVELOP LEADERS — Keep reminding people of the why, support their development, and show what a great meeting looks like.
key_takeaways: 5 phases, each one builds on the last.
The focus shifts from you to other people.
Phase 5 is leaders building leaders.
Each phase needs different skills.

title: Qualities of Effective Leaders
summary: Honesty, inspiration, competence, support — the qualities people want in a leader.
body:
These are the qualities that make people follow you (from Kouzes & Posner plus the impact booklet):

- HONESTY, INSPIRING, COMPETENT, SUPPORTIVE — the big four.
- POSITIVE ATTITUDE — it changes your day and everyone else's.
- ENTHUSIASM — it spreads, and it motivates.
- GOAL DRIVEN — sets goals for yourself and the team.
- SETS STANDARDS — for sales, service, and work ethic.
- CONSISTENT — performs the same every day.
- RESPONSIBLE — owns the wins and the problems.
- INTEGRITY — builds trust.
- PROBLEM SOLVER — brings solutions, not problems.
- DEDICATED — focused on the team and the business.
- CONSIDERATE — knows what the team needs.
- TEAM ORIENTED — makes people feel they belong.
- POSITIVE IMAGE — looks and acts professional.
- STUDENT MENTALITY — always ready to learn.
- SUPPORTIVE — helps people through the hard days.
- ORGANISED — prepares and plans.
- RESILIENT — gets past obstacles.
key_takeaways: Integrity and honesty come first.
A positive attitude and enthusiasm spread to the team.
Goals plus showing up every day equals results.
Caring about people and staying organised let you lead more of them.

title: Seeing Through a Different Lens
summary: Becoming a leader means your team's results matter more than your own. That's Servant Leadership.
body:
When you step into leadership, the way you look at the role changes:

- Organising yourself becomes organising others
- Building your own skills becomes building people skills
- Your personal results become team performance
- Asking for feedback becomes giving feedback
- Playing for yourself becomes playing for the team

This is called Servant Leadership. Your number one responsibility as a leader is to serve and grow your team.

Your success is now their success. When they win, you win.
key_takeaways: Stop focusing on yourself. Start focusing on your people.
Your team's results are your scoreboard now.
Servant leadership beats ordering people around.
People skills become your main skill.

title: Personal Organisation & Structure
summary: You can't lead others if your own week is a mess. Get yourself organised first.
body:
Before you lead anyone, get your own life in order.

- Build a daily and weekly schedule
- Sort your tasks: high, medium, or low priority
- Use the tools: Weekly Planners, Goal Planners, 12-week Planners, Diaries
- Get good at managing your time and your tasks
- Hand off work the right way when someone else can do it

One rule for any system you build: keep it simple. It should be easy to stick with, easy to follow, and easy for others to copy. If your team can't copy it, it dies with you.
key_takeaways: Organise yourself before you organise anyone else.
Use your planning tools every day.
Do the high-priority stuff first, every time.
Build systems simple enough for others to copy.

title: Setting Goals — Personal & Team (S.M.A.R.T.)
summary: S.M.A.R.T. goals turn wishes into plans. Set them for yourself, then help your team set theirs.
body:
A real goal is S.M.A.R.T.:

- SPECIFIC — say exactly what you want
- MEASURABLE — you can track if you're getting there
- ACTION — write down the steps to get it
- REALISTIC — you can actually hit it
- TIMEFRAME — it has a deadline

Set goals in every part of life: business, finances, lifestyle, health, and relationships.

Mix your timeframes too: short-term (a week or a month), mid-term (a quarter), and long-term (a year or more).

As a leader, you don't just set your own goals. You help your team members set theirs and you help them get there.
key_takeaways: S.M.A.R.T. makes goals clear and keeps you honest.
Set goals in every area of life, not just sales.
Have short, mid, and long-term goals at the same time.
Help your team set their goals too.

title: Helping New People Get Started
summary: A new person's first days decide if they stay. Earn the right to run their intro, then set them up to win.
body:
How a new person gets introduced to the opportunity matters more than almost anything. Here's your part as a leader:

- Know the recruitment and introduction process inside out
- Earn the right to introduce someone. You earn it by being good at what you do, showing up every day, wanting to grow, and looking professional
- Get the materials ready and walk them through the plan for the day
- Out in the field, build a real connection using F.O.R.M. — Family, Occupation, Recreation, Motivation
- Back at the office, give them honest feedback and tell them what comes next

A new person who knows the plan, feels connected, and hears clear feedback comes back tomorrow.
key_takeaways: You earn the right to introduce new people. It's not given.
Use F.O.R.M. to build a real connection fast.
Run a clear intro and a clear debrief, every time.
Your role is to set them up to win.

title: Planning Week 1 for New Team Members
summary: Plan a new BA's first week hour by hour — morning, field, and evening all have a purpose.
body:
A new BA's first week needs a plan for every part of the day.

MORNING:
- Walk through the day and the plan
- E.D.P. Phase 1 plus the checklist
- Start building their first sales presentations
- Show them the office schedules and the sales systems
- Set daily sales and performance goals
- Get them ready for the tough questions and objections they'll hear

IN THE FIELD:
- Keep the conversations coming, all day
- Show them the sales presentation steps yourself
- Coach them on what to fix and how to work the territory

EVENING:
- Run the office return process
- Ask how the day felt — really listen
- Go through the paperwork together
- Talk through what went well and what was hard
- Set their goals for tomorrow before they leave

Do this every day of week one and you build a BA. Skip it and you lose one.
key_takeaways: A planned day 1 sets up a strong week 1.
Plan all three parts: morning, field, evening.
Never let them leave without tomorrow's goals set.
Debrief how they felt, not just their numbers.

title: Developing Team Members to Leadership
summary: When a BA gets steady in sales and understands the business, guide them towards leadership. Your role is to make leadership look worth wanting.
body:
Once someone on your team is getting sign-ups day after day and understands how the business works, start guiding them towards leadership. And here's the big one: make leadership LOOK desirable. If it looks like a grind with no upside, nobody will want it.

What someone needs to move into leadership:
- They act in ways the business respects.
- They're willing to listen, learn, and actually use what they learn.
- They ask questions when they're not sure.
- They can run the processes and systems the right way.
- They get sign-ups day after day, not just one hot week.
- They run a profitable business.

How you help:
- Push their desire to help and coach others.
- Help them set bigger goals than they'd set alone.
- Watch for the natural mentors — the ones people already go to for help. Those are your future leaders.
key_takeaways: Make leadership look worth wanting.
Look for steady sign-ups plus curiosity.
Help them set bigger goals.
Spot the natural mentors early.

title: Strategies for Effective Learning & Coaching (70:20:10)
summary: People learn by doing, not by listening. Build your coaching around the 70:20:10 Principle and Dale's Retention Model.
body:
The 70:20:10 PRINCIPLE says where learning really comes from:

- 70% — doing the work, hands-on
- 20% — learning from other people and networking
- 10% — formal stuff: courses, books, sessions

DALE'S RETENTION MODEL shows how much people actually keep:

- Reading: 10%
- Listening: 20%
- Seeing: 30%
- Seeing and hearing: 50%
- Saying and writing: 70%
- Doing: 90%

So what does that mean for you as a coach? Build your morning, field, and evening sessions around DOING and SAYING. Don't lecture your team — get them talking it back and doing it live. That's where the 70% and 90% live.
key_takeaways: 70% of learning comes from doing the work.
20% comes from other people.
10% comes from formal learning.
People keep 90% of what they do and 10% of what they read.

title: Building Your Team & Enterprise
summary: Get your own house in order first. Then give your team an identity, shared goals, and reasons to feel like a team.
body:
Before you build a team, sort yourself out. Your own game has to be in order first.

Then build your team's identity. Answer these together:
- Who are we?
- Where are we going?
- How will we get there?
- What support do we need?

Then make the team FEEL like a team:
- Hold regular team meetings.
- Put up team production charts so everyone can see the numbers.
- Talk up business plans and goals.
- Celebrate wins — big and small.
- Do team dinners and activities.
- Use promotional material and branding for your team.

Shared goals are what pull everyone in the same direction. When the whole team knows where it's going, every day has a purpose.
key_takeaways: Sort your own game first.
Answer together: who are we, where are we going?
Celebrate wins often.
Shared goals pull everyone the same way.

title: Leadership Relationships
summary: Being a leader is not just running the day — it's building real relationships. Trust is what holds a team together.
body:
As a leader you have two responsibilities at once: get the work done, and build real relationships with your people. You need both. One without the other falls apart.

How to do it:
- Take a real interest in people. Care about them, not just their numbers.
- Give credit where it's due.
- Praise in public, criticise in private. Every time.
- Lead by example. Do what you ask others to do.
- Keep communication open. People should feel they can talk to you.
- Get your team to know each other, not just you.
- No blame games. No cliques.

Trust is the foundation. You can't just ask for trust — you have to show it first. Trust people, and build a team where trust can grow.
key_takeaways: Do the work AND build the relationships.
Praise in public, criticise in private.
Show trust first — it spreads.
No cliques, no blame games.

title: It's All About Attitude
summary: Your attitude is a leader's most important quality. The whole team feels it, good or bad.
body:
A leader's attitude spreads. Whatever you carry, your team catches.

- SET THE TONE — your positivity lifts everyone around you
- PUSH THROUGH HARD TIMES — lead by example and stay positive when it's rough
- LISTEN TO YOUR SELF-TALK — catch negative thoughts and swap them for affirmations
- REWARDS — celebrate wins and milestones out loud
- STAY HEALTHY — look after your body and your head

Attitude matters more than education, CV, charm, or experience.
key_takeaways: Attitude beats everything else.
Your self-talk shapes your results.
Celebrate wins to lift the team.
Health gives you stamina.

title: Continual Improvement
summary: Use your KPIs to keep getting better, and reset your goals the moment you catch yourself in 'GOMO' — going through the motions.
body:
Leaders who want bigger results chase Continuous Improvement — small steps or big breakthroughs, but always moving.

Your KPIs are the tool:
- They measure your success
- They let you watch your own progress
- They keep you accountable

When you go flat — that's 'GOMO', going through the motions — it's time to:
- Reset your goals
- Lock your focus back in
- Refresh your routines
- Get the mojo back
key_takeaways: KPIs drive improvement.
Watch out for GOMO.
Reset your goals when you go flat.
You bring the mojo back — you don't wait for it.

title: Additional Leadership Tips & Tools
summary: Extra tools for leading people: introverts and extroverts, Circle of Influence, Blake & Mouton's Grid, and switching up your style.
body:
Here are some tools to help you lead different kinds of people.

INTROVERTS & EXTROVERTS. Most people are somewhere in the middle — that's called an ambivert. Rate yourself and rate your team. Knowing where each person sits helps you coach them the right way.

CONCERN vs INFLUENCE. There are things you can control (your Circle of Influence) and things you can't (your Circle of Concern). Put your energy into what you can control. Worrying about the rest just drains you.

BLAKE & MOUTON'S GRID. This maps leadership styles on two things: how much you care about people, and how much you care about the task. See where you land.

LIGHTBULB / LAMPLIGHT / TORCHBEAM COACHING. Lightbulb is coaching broad ideas to everyone. Lamplight is coaching a small group. Torchbeam is fixing one specific behaviour with one person. Go broad first, then narrow.

VARYING STYLES. Some moments need hands-on leading, some need hands-off. Look at Servant Leadership and Situational Leadership — match your style to the person and the moment.
key_takeaways: Learn where each person sits — introvert to extrovert.
Spend energy on your Circle of Influence, not your worries.
Match your style to the person and the moment.
Coach broad first, then narrow it down.
